1.	In 1896, the British began constructing a 1,000-km railway line from the Indian Ocean port of X to the shores of Lake Victoria — a project so absurdly expensive and lethal that British newspapers nicknamed it “the Lunatic Line.” Three years later, the railhead reached an empty, brackish swamp on Maasai grazing land roughly halfway to the lake, and the chief engineer chose it as the spot for a permanent supply depot. The new town took its name Y from a Maasai phrase meaning “place of cool waters.” Eight years later Y replaced X as the colonial capital. Today, it is the only national capital in the world with a full-fledged national park within its boundaries — lions, leopards, rhinos, and giraffes roam against a backdrop of skyscrapers. 2.	In the 11th century CE, this place appears in the historical record as a small village in the shadow of a once-great neighbor that would later be obliterated by Genghis Khan. By the 13th century, it had grown into a modest market town famous for its pomegranates. In 1786, the founder of a new dynasty chose this unremarkable market town as his royal seat, and from there the Qajars ruled for over a century. In November 1943, the world’s three most powerful men — Stalin, Roosevelt, and Churchill — met here in their first wartime summit and agreed to launch what would become D-Day. The city is near Mount Damavand, the highest volcano in Asia. Name this city (10 points). ‎<attached: 00137036-PHOTO-2026-04-30-09-09-59.jpg>
